subject: Chip stocks fell 8 days straight. Blame the debt.
bodyMarkdown:
Canada's September inflation number lands at 8:30 this morning, and it arrives in the middle of the worst run for chip stocks since 2008. Those two things are connected, and the link runs through borrowed money rather than through anything that happened to AI itself.

## What actually broke last week

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed down 3.83% on Friday at 11,137.29, its eighth straight losing session, and Yahoo Finance reported that this is the longest losing streak for chip stocks since October 2008. The index now sits about 15.7% below its October 6 close of 13,217.82. AMD, Micron, Intel and Broadcom each fell roughly 4.5% to 6% on Friday. Nvidia got off lighter, down about 1.4%.

Then there is the part that changed how I read all of this. Earnings were fine. ASML and TSMC both reported strong numbers during the streak. Borrowing costs moved the helpful way too, with the US 10-year Treasury yield falling from 5.27% to 5.09% over those eight sessions. Chip demand did not collapse last week and neither did the cost of money. Something else gave way.

## The lenders moved first

CoreWeave is the clearest tell. It rents out AI computing power, and it borrowed heavily to buy the chips it rents. Bloomberg reported on Wednesday that its unsecured 2032 bonds traded below 80 cents on the dollar, roughly the line where the market starts treating a borrower as distressed, and that yields on its junk bonds reached about 15%. Reuters reported that the cost of insuring that debt through **credit default swaps**, contracts that pay out if a borrower stops paying, passed 1,000 basis points to record highs. Reuters put CoreWeave's total debt near $50 billion. Its interest expense ran $640 million in the second quarter, up from $267 million a year earlier. CEO Mike Intrator called the selloff irrational and said his order backlog more than covers what the company owes. Bloomberg's credit column on Saturday said junk buyers are now freezing out tech borrowers generally.

## Why I am watching the 8:30 print

Canada's squeeze is tighter than the American one. Statistics Canada reported on October 9 that the economy shed 68,000 jobs in September, a second straight monthly drop, with unemployment up to 6.5%. The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25% through seven decisions in a row, and Tiff Macklem said in September that upside risks to inflation have grown. This morning Statistics Canada publishes September CPI. The Canadian Press reported on Friday that a Reuters poll of economists expects 3.2%, up from 3% in August, while RBC's Nathan Janzen expects it held at 3%. Janzen called the October 28 decision live, with a hike possible though not his base case. Falling employment and rising prices at the same time leave Macklem no comfortable move.

## The takeaway

Look past the headline number at 8:30 and go straight to the core measures, because gasoline has been doing most of the work in these prints and the Bank tends to look through oil. A reading at 3.2% or above makes October 28 a real problem for anyone holding a variable mortgage or facing a renewal in the next few months. I would also watch whether any AI builder manages to price new junk debt this week, since one failed deal would tell you more about the next six months than another 3% down day in semis. The chips were never the fragile part of this trade.
